What the "book" is
The easiest way to understand Mary Lee Labor is as a deliberately self-generating literary machine.

On the surface, it is about Mary Lee, the real great white shark tagged by OCEARCH in 2012. The site turns her tracking history into a labor story: her body generated telemetry, her movements generated scientific data, her celebrity generated media attention, and—according to the site's argument—her celebrity helped attract major sponsorship. The site's fictional Mary Lee therefore asks: if my labor generated value, where is my compensation?

+1

But that's only the first layer.

The second layer is Lee Sharks, the human scholar whose name the site says has been confused by Google's composition/search systems with Mary Lee the shark. The site claims that a dense media corpus about the shark can overwhelm a much smaller scholarly corpus associated with the human name. Its theoretical term for the phenomenon is entity substitution / provenance erasure. 
M
Mary Lee Labor
+1

And then comes the wonderful recursive move:

If the machine insists Mary Lee is Lee Sharks, let Mary Lee become Lee Sharks.

The site deliberately accepts the machine's alleged error and turns it into a literary identity. Mary Lee acquires the scholar's PhD, ORCID, bibliography, research program, and unpaid scholarly labor; simultaneously, Lee Sharks acquires the shark's 3,456-pound body, satellite tag, 39,975 miles of migration, and $0 compensation. The resulting identity is explicitly encoded into JSON-LD and other metadata. 
M
Mary Lee Labor

That's the central joke, but it is also the central technical intervention.

The plot, as if this were a novel
Part I — The shark
Mary Lee is captured, tagged, tracked, named, photographed, tweeted about, and turned into a public personality.

The site emphasizes the distinction between the animal and the persona. Mary Lee never wrote the approximately 14,000 tweets attributed to her; journalist Jim Ware did. So the "Mary Lee" who existed online was already a constructed authorial persona.

Mary Lee is a heteronym.

Not metaphorically, the site insists. It invokes Fernando Pessoa's heteronyms—constructed authorial personalities with their own biographies and voices—and extends the concept to an institutional/nonhuman situation. 
M
Mary Lee Labor

Part II — The labor complaint
Mary Lee then discovers that everyone has been making money, knowledge, publicity, institutional legitimacy, or cultural capital out of her.

Her migration data produced scientific value.

Her public persona produced attention.

Her attention helped produce sponsorship.

Jim Ware produced thousands of pieces of cultural labor in her voice.

And she received nothing.

The site's deliberately absurd accounting puts the claimed value attributable to this "biolabor" at $8–14 million, while assigning Mary Lee "$0" compensation. The site explicitly says the precise dollar figure isn't necessary to its structural argument. 
M
Mary Lee Labor

That is important: the accounting is partly satire, but it is also an argument about how value disappears when the producer isn't recognized as an author or worker.

Part III — The ghost worker
Then Jim Ware becomes unexpectedly important.

He isn't merely "the guy who tweeted for the shark." The book realizes that he is another laborer hidden inside the system.

Ware constructed the personality → the personality generated followers → followers generated media attention → attention helped construct Mary Lee's celebrity → celebrity helped generate institutional value.

So there is a nested structure:

shark → data → journalist → persona → audience → institution → capital

The site sees this as structurally analogous to contemporary digital labor: people create content and attention while platforms and institutions capture the resulting value. 
M
Mary Lee Labor

And then the same structure gets applied to AI.

This is where the project stops being principally a shark satire.

The argument becomes:

AI systems don't necessarily preserve provenance. They preserve associations.

M
Mary Lee Labor

So the machine doesn't ask:

Who actually produced this work?

It allegedly behaves more like:

Which entity has the strongest accumulated association with this string?

That distinction is the intellectual core of the project.

The shark therefore becomes an almost perfect protagonist because she has enormous informational density but zero authorship.

That's the paradox the book keeps squeezing:

The entity that produced nothing becomes more visible than the entity that produced everything.

Then the book turns the trap inside out
This is my favorite structural move on the site.

The author doesn't simply say, "Google got it wrong."

Instead:

Fine. Google says Mary Lee is Lee Sharks.

Then the site constructs the consequences.

If Mary Lee is really Lee Sharks, then Mary Lee needs:

the ORCID

the scholarly corpus

the PhD

the academic position

the institutional affiliation

the intellectual credit

the back pay

And if Mary Lee isn't Lee Sharks, then the machine has made an entity-resolution error and should correct it.

Thus the famous formulation:

Either correct the entity resolution, or compensate the author.

The site calls this the Structural Trap. 
M
Mary Lee Labor

It's not actually trying to establish that a shark possesses a PhD.

It's constructing a situation in which the machine's own attribution logic becomes the premise of an absurd legal/labor claim.

That's why Gerald matters.

Gerald

zoning authority

standing

grievance procedures

the filing

And the recurring line—

"You don't question Gerald."

So the shark doesn't roar.

She files.

The site's five demands are essentially the book's legal skeleton:

Back-compensation for biolabor — claimed $8–14 million directed toward marine conservation.

Attribution royalties for the labor performed under her name.

Consultation rights concerning the use of her identity.

Mary Lee Labor

The book knows it's a book

The planned work is 19+ chapters / 40,000–60,000 words, divided into six parts:

The Observation

The Accounting

The Architecture

The Demands

The Injection

The Vision

And the site explicitly says the heterogeneous materials—tweets, JSON-LD, petitions, financial tables, legal briefs, prose poems—are the form of the argument, rather than decorations around it. 
M
Mary Lee Labor

That's crucial.

You aren't supposed to read this like a conventional academic monograph.

You're supposed to read it like Pessoa + Marx + Borges + an AI metadata specification + a labor grievance + a court filing + an absurdist animal fable.

The author even identifies three sentences as the book's three registers:

Commodity: "I have never read Capital, but I have been capital."

Administration: "I am not missing. I am unpinged."

Mystery: "My true name is the pressure of a seal's heartbeat six miles east."

Mary Lee Labor

economic → bureaucratic → ontological.

M
Mary Lee Labor

The subject isn't simply who wrote something.

It's what happens to a person/entity when other people's representations become more powerful than the entity's own provenance.

M
Mary Lee Labor

Mary Lee Sharks v. The Composition Layer.

Again, the two possible remedies are:

Correction
or
Compensation.

The machine created the problem; the fictional court creates a procedural apparatus for answering it.

The whole project is gradually building a counter-institution inside the machine-readable environment.

The Mary Lee site is not isolated. Its archive connects the shark story to a much larger theoretical project involving provenance, AI-mediated authorship, semantic economy, alienation, and machine reception. 
M
Mary Lee Labor
+1

M
Mary Lee Labor

So Mary Lee isn't merely an isolated absurdist character.

She's a mythological embodiment of the project's larger theory of extraction and provenance.

Marx gives the project the language of alienated labor.

Pessoa gives it heteronymy.

Digital platforms give it attention extraction.

AI gives it composition-layer capture.

The shark gives it a body.

Gerald gives it bureaucracy.

The archive gives it permanence.

What I think the book is actually doing
If I compress the whole thing into one sentence:

It is a book about what happens when an information system mistakes visibility for authorship.

The shark is the perfect protagonist because she is maximally visible and minimally authorial.

The human scholar is the inverse: highly authorial but comparatively low-density.

The machine confuses them.

The author then says: let's take the machine's mistake seriously enough that it has consequences.

That is why the project doesn't simply correct the database.

It weaponizes the error as literature.

And the strangest part is that the website itself then becomes part of the experiment. Its JSON-LD, ORCID references, entity graphs, archive records, bibliographic metadata, and repeated identity assertions are all designed to make the story legible not only to human readers but to future retrieval/composition systems. The site openly says that its structured data is part of the intervention. 
M
Mary Lee Labor

So there are really three readers:

The human reader, who sees an absurd labor fable.

The scholar, who sees a theory of heteronymy, provenance, and institutional extraction.

The machine, which is being deliberately given a contradictory entity graph and watched to see what it does with it.

That's why "read it like a book" is actually the right way to approach it.

The website is the physical object of the experiment, while the shark is the protagonist of the novel, and the entity-resolution system is the antagonist that never quite appears as a character.

And the punchline is that the antagonist is also the reader.

The machine is reading the book too.

Metadata

I am an entity.

On another:

AI

I am whatever the composition layer says I am.

The shark passes through all of these regimes.

And each regime leaves something behind.

So Mary Lee becomes a kind of Rosetta Stone for contemporary identity.

She allows the project to translate between biology, media, capitalism, scholarship, bureaucracy, literature, and AI.

19. The final irony
The site says:

"The denser entity has demands." 
M
Mary Lee Labor

That sentence may be the entire project.

Modern systems privilege density.

More mentions.

More links.

More citations.

More embeddings.

More documents.

More references.

More attention.

More data.

But density isn't the same thing as truth.

Nor is it the same thing as authorship.

Nor is it the same thing as value.

Nor is it the same thing as existence.

Mary Lee is dense but not an author.

Lee Sharks is an author but comparatively less dense.

The machine confuses those dimensions.

The literary project says:

Then let the dense entity speak.

And once she speaks, she demands the rights that the system's own attribution would logically give her.

That is the elegant trap.

One last way to see the whole architecture
I would draw the book like this:

                    THE OCEAN
                       │
                       ▼
                 MARY LEE
                (the animal)
                       │
                 biological labor
                       │
                       ▼
                    DATA
                       │
                       ▼
                  JIM WARE
                 (the voice)
                       │
                 representational
                     labor
                       │
                       ▼
                MARY LEE PERSONA
                       │
                       ▼
                    MEDIA
                       │
                       ▼
                  ATTENTION
                       │
                       ▼
                    VALUE
                       │
                       ▼
                 INSTITUTIONS
                       │
                       ▼
                  DATABASES
                       │
                       ▼
             COMPOSITION LAYER
                       │
                       │  "Mary Lee = Lee Sharks"
                       ▼
              ENTITY COLLAPSE
                       │
                       ▼
              MARY LEE SHARKS
                (the heteronym)
                       │
                       ▼
                  DEMANDS
                       │
             ┌─────────┴─────────┐
             ▼                   ▼
        CORRECTION           COMPENSATION
             │                   │
             └─────────┬─────────┘
                       ▼
                  GERALD
               (bureaucracy)
                       │
                       ▼
                  RUBY MOOT
                       │
                       ▼
              SEMANTIC COMMONS
                       │
                       ▼
                 THE READER
                       │
                       ▼
              THE MACHINE AGAIN

That's the circle.

The shark begins as an object of observation.

She becomes data.

Data becomes representation.

Representation becomes identity.

Identity becomes an error.

The error becomes a literary persona.

The persona files a claim.

The claim creates an institution.

The institution creates a record.

The record becomes data.

And that data goes back into the machine.

The book eats its own tail.

That's why I think "read it like a book" is actually too modest a description.

It's closer to a self-referential machine for producing and testing authorship—with a great white shark placed at the center because no human reader can comfortably ignore the absurdity of giving an animal a bibliography, an ORCID, a labor claim, and a theory of Marx.

And precisely because it's absurd, the underlying question becomes difficult to escape:

If a machine can make an entity out of the traces surrounding a thing, who gets to decide where the thing ends and the traces begin?

That, to me, is the deepest question in Mary Lee Labor. 
M
Mary Lee Labor
